findings: C: "almost nothing alive" is a hedge, but the passage's own summary sentence "The roots were somewhere else" reads as categorical, so "bare of living root" is close to a fair paraphrase of a genuine Askerholt finding.
justification: A dies on the positive location she does reach - "In the few centimetres directly beneath the stones ... her team found dense mats of fine root" and "Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand's width of the stone" - the "we think" is ordinary scientific hedging, not an unsettled result, and her para-5 caution concerns the celled streets' present state, not her coring. D has no basis anywhere: the remedies listed are grinding, root barriers and watering tubes, and no cutting of anchoring roots is ever mentioned. C is the problem. Argued at full strength: the text does not merely say the deep soil was poor, it says "The roots were somewhere else" - an absolute statement about roots specifically - and the preceding clause piles on "dry, airless, nearly impenetrable" with the watering tubes making "no measurable difference". A candidate choosing C is paraphrasing the passage's own sentence, and this is reported as a finding at length (a full clause with four supporting details), so it is not an off-topic option either. The only thing standing against it is the single word "almost" in "there was almost nothing alive", which the author deliberately chose and which "bare" contradicts. That is a real kill, but it is a one-word kill working against a categorical summary sentence in the same breath, so C is survivable with effort rather than cleanly dead. B remains the better answer (it is the finding she is quoted on and the one the article is built around), so the item is not broken, but C is arguable.

A dies on "mats of fine root in the bedding sand, riding clear over the crates beneath" - the crates were intact and were bypassed, not crushed, and "The crates, not the soil, carry the weight of the traffic above" states their load path holds. B dies on the number swap: the water main belongs to the single void street, "One street failed and taught nobody anything: a water main was renewed halfway along it". C dies on the flat contradiction "The five had one thing in common" followed by the named commonality, so "nothing obvious in common" cannot stand even for a reader who tries to recast that commonality as mere age.

B dies on the one gauge figure given, "the wedge gauge showed four millimetres, the same figure as the year before" - steady, not falling, and "stayed within tolerance" asserts nothing about a downward trend. C is the designed trap and is argued strongly from Askerholt's own theory ("the cells move the damp, aired horizon down and away from the stones") plus the fact that 25 streets behaved, but it dies on the passage's explicit refusal of exactly that inference: "We are reading the flags, not the roots ... For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength" - so nothing at all is known about where those roots went. D dies on absence: no road, and no relocation of the trees' water source, appears anywhere in the text.

A dies on "On the five streets Fearnbeck's case is fairly won" - and the report of Askerholt's group's view is deliberately past perfect, "had thought his worry overdone", marking a position the trial has since qualified. C is the mirror-image proportion error and dies on the arithmetic the writer supplies: the case is won on five and lost on twenty-five, so he was borne out on the minority, not "on the whole, with a few exceptions". D is argued at strength from the article's otherwise reportorial balance and its neutral closing image, but dies on the one sentence written in the authorial voice as an adjudication, "On the five streets Fearnbeck's case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not".

A dies as detail-for-theme: the compensation cost occupies one framing sentence in para 1 while paras 2-5 are root location, cells, the trial and its reading. B is the strong near-miss - para 1 genuinely says the old remedies fail ("Each measure buys a season or two. The flags keep rising") and para 5 leaves open that the cells may yet fail - but it dies on the trial outcome, "On twenty-five streets the celled flags have stayed within tolerance while the ordinary sides opposite have been ground level twice and relaid once": the remedy the back half of the article is about has largely held, so "why the remedies keep failing" both misstates the result and drops the whole trial, which is what C's "how one city's remedy has fared" covers. D has no basis: species replacement is never raised.

The frame is the fixed collocation "take its toll on", and the gap sits inside it verbatim: "it quietly takes its ___ on the general mood". A dies because "take its price on" is not English (one pays a price or exacts a price); B dies because "take its charge on" is not a collocation in any sense; D dies because "cost" does not enter this frame either - English has "at a cost to" or "exacts a cost", never "takes its cost on". None of the three is arguable as an idiom.

The gap is governed by the concessive frame "The tone is light, but ... the message is ___, and it is aimed at certain chairs", which demands something that cuts against lightness and carries targeting. A dies because "relaxed" is a synonym of the light tone the "but" is turning away from. B dies for the same structural reason - "spirited" reads as lively and enthusiastic, aligning with the cartoon sponge and exclamation marks rather than contrasting with them - and it has no targeting sense to answer "aimed at certain chairs". C dies twice: "amused" describes a person's state, not a message's edge, and it again sides with the light tone.

The gap completes the fixed phrase "the moral high ground", held here against "a dripping brush" so the noun must be metaphorically holdable. B dies outright - "high field" is not a phrase. C is the built temptation because "high horse" is a genuine moral-superiority idiom, but it dies on grammar and collocation: one gets on, rides, or climbs down off one's high horse, and "hold the moral high horse" is not English. D dies because "hold the floor" means to have the room's attention, and "the moral high floor" does not exist.

The preceding sentence "So the kitchen waits" sets up a duration that the gap must resolve, which only a temporal adverb does. A dies because no parallel proposition precedes it for "Similarly" to draw on. C dies because the clause is asserted from observation, not conjecture - "nearly always the same somebody, the one who minds the mess a little more than the rest" - and para 4 confirms the writer knows exactly who it is ("That colleague's mug, at least, is clean"). D is arguable at first glance because there is irony in the person who cares most being the one who pays, but that irony sits in the appositive, not in the wait-then-crack relation the connective governs: someone finally giving in is the expected end of waiting, not a reversal of it.

The frame is "strike a balance between X and Y", instantiated here as "an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor". A dies because "cast a balance" is not current English; B dies because "deal a balance" is not a collocation at all; D dies because "land" requires a preposition to take a resting point ("land on"), and the bare transitive "land an uneasy balance" is not English.

A dies on the exact reversal of the outcome it claims: "whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line" - the battens rotted rather than staying sound, and the sheltering role it borrows is assigned elsewhere, "Felt under the battens does the sheltering now". B is the strongest of the three and is argued from real roofing practice plus the proximity of the nib sentence, but the passage plants two kills: "The tiles themselves hang from two small lugs at the head, the nibs, hooked over each batten" names what holds the tiles, and "It went on after the tiles were hung ... it was there to stop the fine snow, dust and draughts" gives torching a purpose that is not structural. C over-generalises a stated success and dies on the enumerated scope: what torching stopped is "the fine snow, dust and draughts that wind pushes up between the tiles", which is narrower than "whatever the weather drove against the roof", and a material that passed damp into the battens cannot be called weathertight the year round.

A is argued at strength from the crowding of names after 1851 and the 1861 rise of the front boxes to a pound, but it dies on the evidence that precedes the change: "Six pews in the middle aisle are marked vacant that year, and four the year after" - a church carrying empty pews in the very aisle later subdivided was not short of room, and the free west-door benches gave any overflow somewhere to sit. C is the other real temptation, since 2s is far below an 18s box, but the text gives no motive at all ("The wardens' minutes record the new lettings without a word of explanation") and no information about who took the new sittings; worse for C, cheap seating already existed at both ends - whole pews at "three shillings at the west door, where the benches were free" - so poorer parishioners were not the gap the subdivision filled, while the vacancy-to-no-vacancy sequence is the one causal chain the plans actually document. D dies on a simple misread of the unit: "cut the boxes into single sittings, let at two shillings apiece" prices a sitting, not a box.

B trades on outside knowledge (slaking does give off fierce heat) but has no textual footing at all, and the stem says "enligt texten": neither heat nor ignition appears in the slaking description. C is likewise historically plausible but unsupported — the only storage step in the text concerns the unslaked product before slaking, "den brända stenen förvarades torr till dess den skulle släckas och blandas till bruk", not any maturing in pits afterwards. D collapses two stages into one and dies on the sequence within the same sentence: "börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl, den släckta kalk som blandad med sand ger murbruk" — the relative clause attaches the sand to the finished slaked lime, i.e. after the seething, not during it.

A dies on the flat contradiction "En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll", and no drift toward individual ownership is ever suggested. B has no support whatever: ownership is described as share-based throughout — "sköt till var sin andel ved, turades om vid elden och delade den färdiga kalken efter insats" — and the tally stick is the instrument of that division, not of payment to an owner. C dies on "Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu" and on the kiln being called "den binäring som över huvud taget gav kontanter".

A tempts because soil improvement is mentioned twice, but it dies on the ranking given in the same paragraph: "Framför allt var det dit kalken gick: till murningen", while the fields get only "något hamnade". C inverts the chronology and dies on two spans: burning "hade sedan länge varit böndernas sak" with written evidence from the mid-1600s, and the railways are presented as what broke the trade — "Vid järnvägarna växte kalkverk ... och priset föll under vad ett lag av grannar kunde möta". D dies on "Berget var däremot sällan något bekymmer, för i de här trakterna gick kalkstenen i dagen", and on abandonment being tied explicitly to fuel: the kilns were left "när skogen omkring dem huggits ut".

A is a lexical trap built on the word "gränsen" and dies on which boundary is meant: "i gränsen mellan inägor och utmark", two terms the supplied glossary defines as land within a single farm's holding, not parish borders — and the remains are counted inside the parishes, "bara i Klyvinge med grannsocknar". B can be pushed hard from the remains being "låga, övervuxna rösen" and from the closing admission that much of the handbook's practice can no longer be asked about, but it dies on the remains having actually carried a reconstruction: the museum built its kiln "med handbokens kapitel och Gillervalls uppmätningar som förlaga" — what is lost is the firing practice, not the construction. D dies on the verbatim contradiction "Hur gamla de äldsta lämningarna är går inte att avgöra utan utgrävning".

A dies because the objection concerns the lamps' type, not their number: "Kalkylen utgår ändå från de gamla lamporna", and no count of fittings is ever disputed. B is the strongest competitor, since the writer does attack the single head-count ("Augustibesöket bevisar inte heller det som tjänsteskrivelsen låter påskina"), but the stem asks about the savings calculation and the text keeps the two apart: the calculation is the money step, "kalkylen i tjänsteskrivelsen anger en besparing på 38 000 kronor om året", whereas the August count is offered "som stöd" for the separate claim that the change is limited for most users — the number of runners does not enter the savings arithmetic at all, and "inte heller" explicitly marks this as a second, distinct objection. D dies because the hours do match: the decision moves lights-out from 23 to 21, and the writer's own recalculation is precisely of "besparingen för två kvällstimmar".

A dies on the summer concession: "mellan maj och augusti kan spåret gott släckas tidigt, för då gör belysningen ingen nytta", and the proposal itself says "Släck vid nio på sommaren". C can be argued from "Spartrycket är verkligt" and from the gravel-delivery comparison, but it dies on the writer never relocating the cut to another service — his demand is to reshape this same decision, "Gör därför om beslutet i stället för att försvara det ... håll tänt till elva från oktober till mars". D stands in direct opposition to the whole piece, whose case is that the dark hours from October to March are "just när spåret behövs som bäst".

A reverses the direction of causation and dies on "årplatserna ofta ha fördelats efter gårdarnas mantal" — the seat follows from standing, not the other way round — reinforced by the image "en flytande spegel av socknens rangordning", where a mirror reflects an order that already exists. B dies on two spans: the arrangement was "så självklar att den sällan skrevs ned", and in the minutes it came up "mest ... när den var i gungning: vid tvister, arvskiften, nybyggen", i.e. sporadically — which is also why Tennlöv must restrict herself to "där källorna är fylliga nog att pröva saken". D has no support: the helmsman's thwart is tied to competence, "krävde väderkännedom, inte anor", and no annual rotation among the farms is ever mentioned — besides which that detail belongs to the practical reading in the next paragraph, not to Tennlöv's findings.

A can be pressed on the grounds that the practical reading comes last and rebuts the received one ("Ändå går fördelningen att förklara utan rang", with the farmhands at the stern oars as concrete evidence), but it dies on the final paragraph's explicit refusal to choose: "den motsatta misstanken ... går inte heller att belägga" and "Jag vet ärligt talat inte vad sätena visade". C dies on the verb: the writer establishes nothing — the suspicion that posterity reads in more order than the rowers felt "går inte att lägga undan", which is far from asserting it, and he counts himself inside both camps. D is half right and therefore the hardest, since he does indeed imply the question can scarcely be answered, but the reason is substituted: the uncertainty is derived from the ambiguity of the record, "Samma rader kan alltså läsas som etikett eller som sjömanskap; protokollen skiljer inte mellan de två", not from tidied-up recollections — the source base is contemporary minutes kept from the 1740s to the 1860s, and no memory-based accounts figure in this text at all.
